chapters.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: On reaching Moscow after her meeting with Rostov, Princess Mary had found her nephew there with his tutor, and a letter from Prince Andrew giving her instructions on how to reach her Aunt Malvintseva in Voronezh. That feeling akin to temptation which had tormented her during her father's illness, since his death, and especially since her meeting with Rostov, was smothered by the arrangements for the journey, anxiety about her brother, settling in a new house, meeting new people, and attending to her nephew's education. She was sad. Now, after a month in quiet surroundings, she felt more and more deeply the loss of her father—a loss associated in her mind with the ruin of Russia. She was agitated and constantly tortured by the thought of the dangers threatening her brother, the only close person now remaining to her. She worried too about her nephew's education, for which she had always felt herself inadequate. But in the depths of her soul she felt at peace—a peace arising from the knowledge that she had suppressed those personal dreams and hopes that had been on the point of awakening within her, connected to her meeting with Rostov.

The day after her party, the governor's wife came to see Malvintseva, and after discussing her plan with the aunt, remarked that though under present circumstances a formal engagement was of course out of the question, the young people might still be brought together and could get to know one another. Malvintseva expressed approval, and the governor's wife began to speak of Rostov in Mary's presence, praising him and telling how he had blushed when Princess Mary's name was mentioned. But Princess Mary experienced a painful rather than joyful feeling—her mental peace was destroyed, and desires, doubts, self-reproach, and hopes reawakened.

During the two days before Rostov called, Princess Mary continually thought about how she ought to behave toward him. First she decided not to come to the drawing room when he called to see her aunt—that it would not be proper for her, in her deep mourning, to receive visitors; then she thought this would be rude after what he had done for her; then it occurred to her that her aunt and the governor's wife had intentions concerning her and Rostov—their looks and words sometimes seemed to confirm this suspicion—then she told herself that only she, with her sinful nature, could think this of them: they could not forget that in her position, while still wearing deep mourning, such matchmaking would be an insult to her and to her father's memory. Assuming she did go down to see him, Princess Mary imagined the words he would say to her and what she would say to him, and these words sometimes seemed undeservedly cold and then too full of meaning. More than anything she feared that the confusion she felt might overwhelm her and betray her as soon as she saw him.

But when on Sunday after church the footman announced in the drawing room that Count Rostov had called, the princess showed no confusion. Only a slight blush came to her cheeks and her eyes lit up with a new and radiant light.
"You have met him, Aunt?" said she in a calm voice, unable herself to understand how she could be so outwardly calm and natural.

When Rostov entered the room, the princess dropped her eyes for an instant, as if to give the visitor time to greet her aunt, and then, just as Nicholas turned to her, she raised her head and met his gaze with shining eyes. With a movement full of dignity and grace she half rose with a smile of pleasure, held out her slender, delicate hand, and began to speak in a voice in which, for the first time, new deep womanly notes vibrated. Mademoiselle Bourienne, who was in the drawing room, looked at Princess Mary in bewildered surprise. A consummate flirt herself, she could not have maneuvered better on meeting a man she wished to attract.
"Either black is particularly becoming to her, or she really has greatly improved without my noticing it. And above all, what tact and grace!" thought Mademoiselle Bourienne.

Had Princess Mary been capable of reflection at that moment, she would have been more surprised than Mademoiselle Bourienne at the change in herself. From the moment she recognized that dear, loved face, a new life force took possession of her and compelled her to speak and act apart from her own will. From the moment Rostov entered, her face was suddenly transformed. It was as if a light had been kindled in a carved and painted lantern, and the intricate, skillful, artistic work on its sides—that previously seemed dark, coarse, and meaningless—was suddenly revealed in unexpected and striking beauty. For the first time, all that pure, spiritual, inward labor through which she had lived appeared on the surface. All her inner work, her dissatisfaction with herself, her suffering, her striving for goodness, her gentleness, love, and self-sacrifice—all this now shone in those radiant eyes, in her delicate smile, and in every feature of her gentle face.

Rostov saw all this as clearly as if he had known her his whole life. He felt that the person before him was quite different from, and better than, anyone he had met before, and above all better than himself.

Their conversation was very simple and unimportant. They spoke of the war, and like everyone else unconsciously exaggerated their sorrow about it; they spoke of their last meeting—Nicholas trying to change the subject—they talked of the governor's kind wife, of Nicholas's relatives, and of Princess Mary's.

She did not talk about her brother, steering the conversation away as soon as her aunt mentioned Andrew. Evidently she could speak of Russia's misfortunes with a certain artificiality, but her brother was too close to her heart and she neither could nor would speak lightly of him. Nicholas noticed this, as he noticed every shade of Princess Mary's character with an observation unusual for him, and everything confirmed his conviction that she was a quite unusual and extraordinary person. Nicholas blushed and grew confused when people spoke to him about the princess (as she did when he was mentioned) and even when he thought of her, but in her presence he felt completely at ease and said not at all what he had prepared, but what, quite naturally, occurred to him at the moment.

When a pause occurred during his short visit, Nicholas, as is usual when there are children, turned to Prince Andrew's little son, caressing him and asking whether he would like to be a hussar. He took the boy on his knee, played with him, and looked over at Princess Mary. With a softened, happy, shy look she watched the boy she loved in the arms of the man she loved. Nicholas also noticed that look and, as if understanding it, flushed with pleasure and began kissing the boy with good-natured playfulness.

As she was in mourning, Princess Mary did not go out in society, and Nicholas did not think it proper to visit her again; but the governor's wife continued her matchmaking, passing on to Nicholas the flattering things Princess Mary said about him and vice versa, and insisting that he declare himself to Princess Mary. For this purpose she arranged a meeting between the young people at the bishop's house before Mass.
Though Rostov told the governor's wife that he would make no declaration to Princess Mary, he promised to go.

Just as at Tilsit Rostov had not allowed himself to doubt that what everybody considered right was right, so now, after a short but sincere struggle between his effort to arrange his life according to his own sense of justice and his obedient submission to circumstances, he chose the latter and yielded to the power that he felt irresistibly carrying him he knew not where. He knew that after his promise to Sonya it would be what he considered dishonorable to declare his feelings to Princess Mary. And he knew that he would never act dishonorably. But he also knew (or rather felt at the bottom of his heart) that by yielding now to the force of circumstances and to those who were guiding him, he was not only doing nothing wrong but was doing something very important—more important than anything he had ever done in his life.

After meeting Princess Mary, though his daily routine went on as before, all his former amusements lost their charm and he often thought about her. But he never thought about her as he had thought of all the young ladies he had met in society without exception, nor as he had for a long time—and at one point rapturously—thought about Sonya. He had pictured each of those young ladies as almost all honest-hearted young men do, that is, as a possible wife, fitting her in his imagination to all the conditions of married life: a white dressing gown, his wife at the tea table, his wife's carriage, little ones, Mama and Papa, their relations to her, and so on—and these pictures of the future had given him pleasure. But with Princess Mary, to whom they were trying to get him engaged, he could never picture anything of future married life. If he tried, his pictures seemed incongruous and false. It made him afraid.

chapters.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter VII
paragraphs: The dreadful news of the battle of Borodino, of the losses in killed and wounded, and the still more terrible news of the fall of Moscow reached Voronezh in the middle of September. Princess Mary, having learned of her brother's wound only from the official gazette, and having no definite news of him, prepared (so Nicholas heard—he had not seen her again) to set off in search of Prince Andrew.

When he received the news of the battle of Borodino and the abandonment of Moscow, Rostov was not seized with despair, anger, the desire for vengeance, or any feeling of that kind. Instead, everything in Voronezh suddenly seemed dull and tiresome, and he felt an indefinite sense of shame and awkwardness. The conversations he heard seemed insincere; he did not know how to judge all these affairs and felt that only in the regiment would everything become clear again. He hurried to finish buying the horses and often became unreasonably angry with his servant and squadron quartermaster.

A few days before his departure, a special thanksgiving service was held in the cathedral for the Russian victory, and Nicholas was present. He stood a little behind the governor and held himself with military decorum throughout the service, meditating on a great variety of subjects. When the service was over the governor's wife beckoned him to her.
"Have you seen the princess?" she asked, indicating with a nod a lady standing on the opposite side, beyond the choir.

Nicholas immediately recognized Princess Mary—not so much by the profile he saw under her bonnet as by the feeling of concern, shyness, and pity that instantly overcame him. Princess Mary, evidently engrossed in her thoughts, was crossing herself for the last time before leaving the church.

Nicholas looked at her face with surprise. It was the same face he had seen before, with the same general expression of refined inner spiritual effort, but now it was quite differently lit up. There was a touching expression of sorrow, prayer, and hope in it. As had happened before when she was present, Nicholas went up to her without waiting for the governor's wife's prompting and without asking himself whether it was right and proper to address her here in church, and told her he had heard of her trouble and sympathized with his whole soul. As soon as she heard his voice, a vivid glow kindled in her face, lighting up both her sorrow and her joy.

"There is one thing I wanted to tell you, Princess," said Rostov. "It is that if your brother, Prince Andrew Nikolaevich, were not living, the news would have been announced in the gazette at once, since he is a colonel."
The princess looked at him, not grasping what he was saying, but cheered by the expression of regretful sympathy on his face.

"And I have known so many cases of a splinter wound" (the gazette said it was a shell) "either proving fatal at once or being very slight," continued Nicholas. "We must hope for the best, and I am sure..."
Princess Mary interrupted him.

"Oh, that would be so dread..." she began and, prevented by emotion from finishing, bent her head with a movement as graceful as everything she did in his presence, and looking up at him gratefully, went out, following her aunt.

That evening Nicholas did not go out but stayed at home to settle some accounts with the horse dealers. When he had finished that business it was already too late to go anywhere but still too early for bed, and for a long time he paced up and down the room reflecting on his life—something he rarely did.

Princess Mary had made an agreeable impression on him when he had met her in Smolensk province. His having encountered her in such exceptional circumstances, and his mother's having at one time mentioned her as a good match, had drawn his particular attention to her. When he met her again in Voronezh, the impression she made on him was not merely pleasing but powerful. Nicholas had been struck by the peculiar moral beauty he observed in her at this time. He was, however, preparing to leave, and it had not entered his head to regret missing chances to see her. But that day's encounter in the church had, he felt, sunk deeper than was desirable for his peace of mind. That pale, sad, refined face, that radiant look, those gentle, graceful gestures, and especially the deep and tender sorrow expressed in all her features agitated him and stirred his sympathy. In men, Rostov could not bear to see the expression of a higher spiritual life (that was why he did not like Prince Andrew), and he referred to it dismissively as philosophy and dreaminess; but in Princess Mary, that very sorrow which revealed the depth of a whole spiritual world foreign to him was an irresistible attraction.

"She must be a wonderful woman. A real angel!" he said to himself. "Why am I not free? Why was I in such a hurry with Sonya?" And he involuntarily compared the two: the lack of spirituality in the one and the abundance of it in the other—a spirituality he himself lacked and therefore valued most highly. He tried to picture what would happen if he were free. How he would propose to her and how she would become his wife. But no, he could not imagine it. He felt awe, and no clear picture presented itself to his mind. He had long ago pictured a future with Sonya, and it was all clear and simple because it had all been thought out and he knew everything there was in Sonya. But it was impossible to picture a future with Princess Mary, because he did not understand her but simply loved her.
Daydreams about Sonya had something merry and playful in them, but to dream of Princess Mary was always difficult and a little frightening.

"How she prayed!" he thought. "It was plain that her whole soul was in her prayer. Yes, that was the prayer that moves mountains, and I am sure her prayer will be answered. Why don't I pray for what I want?" he suddenly thought. "What do I want? To be free, released from Sonya... She was right," he thought, remembering what the governor's wife had said: "Nothing but misfortune can come of marrying Sonya. Confusion, grief for Mama... business difficulties... confusion, terrible confusion! Besides, I don't love her—not as I should. O God! Release me from this dreadful, inextricable situation!" he suddenly began to pray. "Yes, prayer can move mountains, but one must have faith and not pray as Natasha and I used to as children, that the snow might turn into sugar—and then run out into the yard to see whether it had. No, but I am not praying for trifles now," he thought as he put his pipe down in a corner, and folding his hands, placed himself before the icon. Softened by memories of Princess Mary, he began to pray as he had not done for a long time. Tears were in his eyes and in his throat when the door opened and Lavrushka came in with some papers.
"Blockhead! Why do you come in without being called?" cried Nicholas, quickly changing his posture.
"From the governor," said Lavrushka in a sleepy voice. "A courier has arrived and there's a letter for you."
"Well, all right, thanks. You can go!"

Nicholas took the two letters, one from his mother and the other from Sonya. He recognized them by the handwriting and opened Sonya's first. He had read only a few lines when he turned pale and his eyes opened wide with fear and joy.
"No, it's not possible!" he cried aloud.

Unable to sit still, he paced up and down the room holding the letter and reading it. He glanced through it, then read it again, and then once more, and standing still in the middle of the room raised his shoulders, stretching out his hands, with his mouth wide open and his eyes fixed. What he had just been praying for with confidence that God would hear him had come to pass; but Nicholas was as astonished as if it were something extraordinary and unexpected, and as if the very fact that it had happened so quickly proved it had come not from God—to whom he had prayed—but by some ordinary coincidence.

This unexpected and, as it seemed to Nicholas, completely voluntary letter from Sonya freed him from the knot that had bound him and from which there had seemed no escape. She wrote that the recent unfortunate events—the loss of nearly all the Rostovs' Moscow property—and the countess's repeatedly expressed wish that Nicholas should marry Princess Bolkonskaya, together with his silence and coldness of late, had all combined to make her decide to release him from his promise and set him completely free.

It would be too painful to me to think that I might be a cause of sorrow or conflict in the family that has been so good to me (she wrote), and my love has no aim but the happiness of those I love; so, Nicholas, I beg you to consider yourself free, and to be assured that, in spite of everything, no one can love you more than does
Your Sonya

Both letters were written from Troitsa. The other, from the countess, described their last days in Moscow, their departure, the fire, and the destruction of all their property. In this letter the countess also mentioned that Prince Andrew was among the wounded traveling with them; his condition was very critical, but the doctor said there was now more hope. Sonya and Natasha were nursing him.

Next day Nicholas took his mother's letter and went to see Princess Mary. Neither he nor she said a word about what "Natasha nursing him" might mean, but thanks to this letter Nicholas suddenly became almost as intimate with the princess as if they were relatives.
The following day he saw Princess Mary off on her journey to Yaroslavl, and a few days later left to rejoin his regiment.

chapters.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter VIII
paragraphs: Sonya's letter from Troitsa, which had come as an answer to Nicholas's prayer, was prompted by this: the thought of getting Nicholas married to an heiress occupied the old countess's mind more and more. She knew that Sonya was the chief obstacle to this, and Sonya's life in the countess's house had grown harder and harder, especially after they received a letter from Nicholas telling of his meeting with Princess Mary in Bogucharovo. The countess let no opportunity slip for making humiliating or cruel remarks to Sonya.

But a few days before they left Moscow, moved and excited by all that was going on, the countess called Sonya to her and, instead of reproaching and making demands, tearfully begged her to sacrifice herself and repay all that the family had done for her by breaking off her engagement with Nicholas.
"I shall not be at peace till you promise me this."

Sonya burst into hysterical tears and replied through her sobs that she would do anything and was prepared for anything, but gave no actual promise and could not bring herself to do what was demanded of her. She had to sacrifice herself for the family that had raised her. Sacrificing herself for others was Sonya's habit. Her position in the house was such that only through sacrifice could she prove her worth, and she was accustomed to this and loved doing it. But in all her previous acts of self-sacrifice she had been happily aware that they raised her in her own esteem and in that of others, making her more worthy of Nicholas, whom she loved more than anything in the world. But now they wanted her to sacrifice the very thing that was the entire reward for her self-sacrifice and the whole meaning of her life. And for the first time she felt bitterness against those who had been her benefactors only to torment her more; she felt jealous of Natasha, who had never experienced anything of the sort, had never needed to sacrifice herself, but made others sacrifice themselves for her, and yet was loved by everybody. And for the first time Sonya felt that out of her pure, quiet love for Nicholas, a passionate feeling was beginning to grow—stronger than principle, virtue, or religion. Under the influence of this feeling, Sonya—whose life of dependence had taught her to be secretive—having answered the countess in vague general terms, avoided further discussion and resolved to wait until she saw Nicholas, not to set him free but on the contrary, at that meeting, to bind him to her forever.

The bustle and terror of the Rostovs' last days in Moscow stifled the gloomy thoughts that oppressed Sonya. She was glad to find escape in practical activity. But when she heard of Prince Andrew's presence in their house, despite her sincere pity for him and for Natasha, she was seized by a joyful and superstitious feeling that God did not intend her to be separated from Nicholas. She knew that Natasha loved no one but Prince Andrew and had never stopped loving him. She knew that being thrown together again under such terrible circumstances, they would fall in love once more, and that Nicholas would then be unable to marry Princess Mary, as they would be too closely connected by family ties. Despite all the terror of what had happened during those last days and during the first days of their journey, this feeling that Providence was intervening in her personal affairs cheered Sonya.
At the Troitsa monastery the Rostovs first broke their journey for a whole day.

Three large rooms were assigned to them in the monastery hostelry, one of which was occupied by Prince Andrew. The wounded man was much better that day, and Natasha was sitting with him. In the next room sat the count and countess, respectfully conversing with the prior, who was visiting them as old acquaintances and benefactors of the monastery. Sonya was there too, tormented by curiosity about what Prince Andrew and Natasha were talking about. She heard the sound of their voices through the door. That door opened and Natasha came out, looking excited. Not noticing the monk who had risen to greet her and was drawing back the wide sleeve on his right arm, she went straight to Sonya and took her hand.
"Natasha, what are you doing? Come here!" said the countess.
Natasha went up to the monk for his blessing, and he advised her to pray for the help of God and His saint.
As soon as the prior withdrew, Natasha took her friend by the hand and went with her into the unoccupied room.

"Sonya, will he live?" she asked. "Sonya, how happy I am, and how unhappy!... Sonya, dear, everything is as it used to be. If only he lives! He cannot... because... because... of..." and Natasha burst into tears.
"Yes! I knew it! Thank God!" murmured Sonya. "He will live."

Sonya was no less agitated than her friend—by Natasha's fear and grief and by her own personal feelings, which she shared with no one. Sobbing, she kissed and comforted Natasha. "If only he lives!" she thought. Having wept, talked, and wiped away their tears, the two friends went together to Prince Andrew's door. Natasha opened it cautiously and glanced into the room, Sonya standing beside her at the half-open door.
Prince Andrew was lying propped high on three pillows. His pale face was calm, his eyes closed, and they could see his steady breathing.
"Oh, Natasha!" Sonya suddenly almost screamed, catching her companion's arm and stepping back from the door.
"What? What is it?" asked Natasha.
"It's that, that..." said Sonya, with a white face and trembling lips.
Natasha softly closed the door and went with Sonya to the window, not yet understanding what she was telling her.
"You remember," said Sonya with a solemn and frightened expression, "you remember when I looked in the mirror for you... at Otradnoe at Christmas? Do you remember what I saw?"
"Yes, yes!" cried Natasha, opening her eyes wide and vaguely recalling that Sonya had told her something about Prince Andrew whom she had seen lying down.

"You remember?" Sonya went on. "I saw it then and told everybody, you and Dunyasha. I saw him lying on a bed," said she, making a gesture with her hand and a lifted finger at each detail, "and that he had his eyes closed and was covered just with a pink quilt, and that his hands were folded," she concluded, convincing herself that the details she had just seen were exactly what she had seen in the mirror.

In fact she had seen nothing then but had mentioned the first thing that came into her head, but what she had invented then now seemed to her as real as any other memory. She not only remembered what she had then said—that he turned to look at her and smiled and was covered with something red—but was firmly convinced that she had seen and said that he was covered with a pink quilt and that his eyes were closed.
"Yes, yes, it really was pink!" cried Natasha, who now thought she too remembered the word pink being used, and saw in this the most extraordinary and mysterious part of the prediction.
"But what does it mean?" she added thoughtfully.
"Oh, I don't know, it's all so strange," replied Sonya, clutching at her head.
A few minutes later Prince Andrew rang and Natasha went to him, but Sonya, feeling unusually excited and touched, remained at the window thinking about the strangeness of what had occurred.
They had an opportunity that day to send letters to the army, and the countess was writing to her son.

"Sonya!" said the countess, raising her eyes from her letter as her niece passed. "Sonya, won't you write to Nicholas?" She spoke in a soft, tremulous voice, and in the weary eyes that looked over her spectacles Sonya read all that the countess meant to convey with these words. Those eyes expressed pleading, shame at having to ask, fear of a refusal, and readiness for merciless hatred in case of such refusal.
Sonya went up to the countess and, kneeling down, kissed her hand.
"Yes, Mama, I will write," said she.

Sonya was softened, excited, and touched by all that had happened that day, especially by the mysterious fulfillment she had just seen of her vision. Now that she knew the renewal of Natasha's relationship with Prince Andrew would prevent Nicholas from marrying Princess Mary, she felt a joyful return of that self-sacrificing spirit she was accustomed to and loved to live by. So with a joyful consciousness of performing a noble deed—interrupted several times by tears that blurred her velvety black eyes—she wrote that touching letter the arrival of which had so amazed Nicholas.

chapters.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter IX
paragraphs: The officer and soldiers who had arrested Pierre treated him with hostility but also with respect in the guardhouse to which he was taken. In their attitude toward him could still be felt both uncertainty as to who he might be—perhaps a very important person—and hostility resulting from their recent personal conflict with him.

But when the guard was relieved next morning, Pierre felt that for the new guard—both officers and men—he was not as interesting as he had been to his captors; and in fact, the second day's guard did not recognize in this big, stout man in a peasant coat the vigorous person who had fought so desperately with the marauder and the escort and had uttered those solemn words about saving a child. They saw in him only Prisoner No. 17 of the captured Russians, arrested and held for some reason by order of the Higher Command. If they noticed anything remarkable about Pierre, it was only his untroubled, meditative concentration and thoughtfulness, and the way he spoke French, which struck them as surprisingly good. Despite this, he was placed that day with the other arrested suspects, as the separate room he had occupied was needed by an officer.

All the Russians confined with Pierre were men of the lowest class, and recognizing him as a gentleman, they all avoided him—especially as he spoke French. Pierre felt sad hearing them make fun of him.

That evening he learned that all these prisoners (he probably among them) were to be tried for arson. On the third day he was taken with the others to a house where a French general with a white mustache sat with two colonels and other Frenchmen with scarves on their arms. With the precision and formality customary in addressing prisoners—intended to preclude human frailty—Pierre, like the others, was questioned as to who he was, where he had been, with what purpose, and so on.

These questions, like questions at trials in general, left the essence of the matter aside, shut out the possibility of that essence being revealed, and were designed only to form a channel through which the judges wished the answers to flow so as to lead to the desired result—namely, a conviction. As soon as Pierre began to say anything that didn't fit that aim, the channel was removed and the water flowed to waste. Pierre felt, moreover, what the accused always feel at their trial—perplexity as to why these questions were put to him. He had a feeling that it was only out of condescension or a kind of courtesy that this device of placing a channel was employed. He knew he was in these men's power, that only by force had they brought him there, that force alone gave them the right to demand answers to their questions, and that the sole purpose of this assembly was to convict him. And so, since they had the power and wish to convict him, this procedure of inquiry and trial seemed unnecessary. It was obvious that any answer would lead to conviction. When asked what he was doing when arrested, Pierre replied in a rather dramatic manner that he was returning a child he had saved from the flames to its parents. Why had he fought the marauder? Pierre answered that he "was protecting a woman" and that "to protect a woman being attacked was the duty of every man; that..." They interrupted him, for this was not to the point. Why was he in the yard of a burning house, where witnesses had seen him? He replied that he had gone out to see what was happening in Moscow. Again they interrupted him: they had not asked where he was going, but why he was found near the fire. Who was he? they asked, repeating their first question, which he had declined to answer. Again he said he could not answer it.
"Put that down. That's bad... very bad," sternly remarked the general with the white mustache and red, flushed face.
On the fourth day, fires broke out on the Zubovsky rampart.

Pierre and thirteen others were moved to the coach house of a merchant's house near the Crimean bridge. On his way through the streets, Pierre was choked by the smoke that seemed to hang over the whole city. Fires were visible on all sides. He did not then realize the significance of the burning of Moscow, and looked at the fires with horror.

He spent four days in the coach house near the Crimean bridge and during that time learned from the talk of the French soldiers that all those confined there were awaiting a decision from the marshal—any day now. Which marshal, Pierre could not find out from the soldiers. Evidently for them "the marshal" represented a very high and rather mysterious power.
These first days, before the eighth of September when the prisoners were brought up for a second examination, were the hardest of all for Pierre.

chapters.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter X
paragraphs: On the eighth of September an officer—a very important one, judging by the respect the guards showed him—entered the coach house where the prisoners were. This officer, probably someone on the staff, held a paper in his hand and called over all the Russians there, naming Pierre as "the man who does not give his name." Glancing casually and indifferently at all the prisoners, he ordered the officer in charge to have them decently dressed and tidied up before taking them to the marshal. An hour later a squad of soldiers arrived and Pierre with thirteen others was led to the Virgin's Field. It was a fine day, sunny after rain, and the air was unusually pure. The smoke did not hang low as on the day Pierre had been taken from the guardhouse on the Zubovsky rampart, but rose through the clear air in columns. No flames were seen, but columns of smoke rose on all sides, and all Moscow, as far as Pierre could see, was one vast charred ruin. On all sides there were waste spaces with only stoves and chimney stacks still standing, and here and there the blackened walls of some brick houses. Pierre gazed at the ruins and did not recognize districts he had known well. Here and there he could see churches that had not burned. The Kremlin, undestroyed, gleamed white in the distance with its towers and the belfry of Ivan the Great. The domes of the New Convent of the Virgin glittered brightly, and its bells were ringing particularly clearly. These bells reminded Pierre that it was Sunday and the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin. But there seemed to be no one to celebrate this holiday: everywhere were blackened ruins, and the few Russians to be seen were tattered, frightened people who tried to hide when they saw the French.

It was plain that the Russian nest was ruined and destroyed, but in place of the Russian order of life that had been destroyed, Pierre unconsciously sensed that a quite different, firm, French order had been established over this ruined nest. He felt this in the looks of the soldiers who, marching in regular ranks briskly and cheerfully, were escorting him and the other prisoners; he felt it in the looks of an important French official in a carriage and pair driven by a soldier, whom they met on the way. He felt it in the merry sounds of regimental music from the left side of the field, and felt and realized it especially from the list of prisoners the French officer had read out that morning. Pierre had been taken by one set of soldiers and led first to one and then to another place with dozens of other men, and it seemed that they might have forgotten him or mixed him up with the others. But no: the answers he had given when questioned had come back to him in his designation as "the man who does not give his name," and under that label, which seemed to Pierre terrible, they were now leading him somewhere with unhesitating confidence on their faces—assurance that he and all the other prisoners were exactly the ones they wanted and that they were being taken to the proper place. Pierre felt himself to be an insignificant chip fallen among the wheels of a machine whose workings he did not understand but which was operating smoothly.

He and the other prisoners were taken to the right side of the Virgin's Field, to a large white house with an immense garden not far from the convent. This was Prince Shcherbatov's house, where Pierre had often been in better days, and which, as he learned from the talk of the soldiers, was now occupied by the marshal, the Duke of Eckmuhl (Davout).

They were taken to the entrance and led into the house one by one. Pierre was the sixth to enter. He was conducted through a glass gallery, an anteroom, and a hall—all familiar to him—into a long low study at whose door stood an adjutant.

Davout, with spectacles perched on his nose, sat bent over a table at the far end of the room. Pierre went close up to him, but Davout, evidently consulting a paper before him, did not look up. Without raising his eyes, he said in a low voice:
"Who are you?"

Pierre was silent because he was incapable of uttering a word. To him Davout was not merely a French general, but a man notorious for his cruelty. Looking at that cold face as Davout sat like a stern schoolmaster willing to wait for an answer, Pierre felt that every instant of delay might cost him his life; but he did not know what to say. He did not dare to repeat what he had said at his first examination, yet to reveal his rank and position was dangerous and embarrassing. So he was silent. But before he had decided what to do, Davout raised his head, pushed his spectacles back on his forehead, narrowed his eyes, and looked intently at him.
"I know that man," he said in a cold, measured tone, evidently calculated to frighten Pierre.
The chill that had been running down Pierre's back now seized his head like a vise.
"You cannot know me, General. I have never seen you..."
"He is a Russian spy," Davout interrupted, addressing another general who was present but whom Pierre had not noticed.
Davout turned away. With an unexpected resonance in his voice, Pierre began rapidly:
"No, monseigneur," he said, suddenly remembering that Davout was a duke. "No, monseigneur, you cannot have known me. I am a militia officer and have not left Moscow."
"Your name?" asked Davout.
"Bezukhov."
"What proof have I that you are not lying?"
"Monseigneur!" exclaimed Pierre, not in an offended but in a pleading voice.

Davout looked up and gazed intently at him. For some seconds they looked at one another, and that look saved Pierre. Apart from conditions of war and law, that look established human relations between the two men. In that moment an immense number of things passed dimly through both their minds, and they realized that they were both children of humanity and were brothers.

At first glance, when Davout had only raised his head from the papers where human lives were indicated by numbers, Pierre was merely a case, and Davout could have shot him without burdening his conscience. But now he saw in him a human being. He reflected for a moment.
"How can you prove to me that you are telling the truth?" said Davout coldly.
Pierre remembered Ramballe, and named him and his regiment and the street where the house was.
"You are not what you say," returned Davout.
In a trembling, faltering voice Pierre began giving proofs of the truth of his statements.
But at that moment an adjutant entered and reported something to Davout.
Davout brightened at the adjutant's news and began buttoning up his uniform. He seemed to have completely forgotten Pierre.

When the adjutant reminded him of the prisoner, he jerked his head in Pierre's direction with a frown and ordered him to be led away. But where they were to take him Pierre did not know: back to the coach house, or to the place of execution his companions had pointed out as they crossed the Virgin's Field.
He turned his head and saw that the adjutant was putting another question to Davout.
"Yes, of course!" replied Davout, but what this "yes" meant, Pierre did not know.

Pierre could not afterward remember how he went, whether it was far, or in what direction. His faculties were completely numb; he was stupefied, and noticing nothing around him, he went on moving his legs as the others did till they all stopped and he stopped too. The only thought in his mind was: who had really sentenced him to death? Not the men on the commission that had first examined him—not one of them wished to or, evidently, could have done it. It was not Davout, who had looked at him in such a human way. In another moment Davout would have realized that he was doing wrong, but just then the adjutant had come in and interrupted him. The adjutant, too, had evidently had no evil intent, though he might have refrained from coming in. Then who was executing him, killing him, depriving him of life—him, Pierre, with all his memories, aspirations, hopes, and thoughts? Who was doing this? And Pierre felt that it was no one.
It was a system—a convergence of circumstances.
A system of some sort was killing him—Pierre—depriving him of life, of everything, annihilating him.
